thread.title: PCOS reclassification to PMOS hopes to improve diagnosis, treatment options and funding
thread.title_full: PCOS reclassification to PMOS hopes to improve diagnosis, treatment options and funding

author: Hannah Bodnar
title: PCOS reclassification to PMOS hopes to improve diagnosis, treatment options and funding
text:
After 14 years of global collaboration, researchers, doctors and the broader medical community reached a consensus to reclassify polycystic ovary syndrome — a disease affecting%20is%20the%20new%20name%20for%20the%20condition%20previously%20known%20as%20Polycystic%20Ovary%20Syndrome%20(PCOS)%2C%20which%20impacts%201%20in%208%2C%20or%20more%20than%20170%20million%20women%20worldwide.,-More%20than%2050) one in eight women. In a study00717-8/fulltext) published May 12, the disorder was renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, reflecting a more comprehensive understanding of the diseases’ complex hormonal and metabolic nature.
PMOS is a common hormonal disorder affecting the reproductive system in individuals assigned female at birth. It is diagnosed in reproductive-age women based on the presence of at least two of the three Rotterdam criteria. The three criteria include hyperandrogenism — excess male hormones which can be detected through blood tests or physical signs such as a deepened voice, male-pattern hair loss and facial hair — irregular menstrual periods and polycystic ovarian morphology, characterized by an excess of follicles in the ovaries.
In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Medical School student Evey Aslanian said the condition’s former name is inaccurate because it highlights a symptom affecting only a portion of those with the disease.
“The focus on the polycystic part is very misleading, because not all patients who experienced PMOS actually had cysts in their ovaries,” Aslanian said. “And even then, cyst is a misnomer because they’re follicles; they’re a normal part of what’s in the ovary. There are just more of them (that are) immature than there should be.”
Aslanian said the name PCOS also ignores hyperandrogenism and irregular periods caused by the disease. In an email to The Daily, Information assistant professor Megan Threats wrote the new title acknowledges that the disease causes multisystem health impacts beyond the ovaries.
“While the previous name focused on the ovaries, the new name reflects substantial research and evidence synthesis that highlight the condition’s endocrine and metabolic impact,” Threats wrote. “So adding the term ‘metabolic’ acknowledges the risk of type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease that may come with the condition. Changing ‘polycystic’ to ‘polyendocrine’ highlights other broader features of the condition, such as endocrine abnormalities and elevated androgens.”
At a 2012 PCOS workshop held by the National Institutes of Health Office of Disease Prevention, panelists recognized the previous name’s potential to delay diagnosis and proposed a name change. The workshop inspired international advocacy for a more accurate and symptom-based name. While PMOS has not yet been officially reclassified, researchers have laid out a three-year plan for its official recognition by international bodies — including the World Health Organization.
The name’s prior focus on ovarian cysts left patients and doctors underinformed on the condition’s broader impacts, contributing to 70% of affected individuals remaining undiagnosed.
In an interview with The Daily, Samantha Schon, assistant professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the University of Michigan, said she hopes the reclassification will improve diagnostic accuracy.
“This has been a problem for a really long time,” Schon said. “It led to a lot of women having delayed diagnosis or misdiagnosis, because women would say, ‘I have a history of ovarian cysts. I’ve been seen in the ER for ovarian cysts,’ and that’s something totally different than PCOS.”
Aslanian said the change may also increase research funding for PMOS by dismantling assumptions about the condition’s severity and calling attention to its severe multisystem impacts.
“Instead of focusing on the ovarian aspect of the syndrome — which relegates it to a women’s health issue where it doesn’t get very much research or research funding and also minimizes the symptoms associated — we wanted to rename it so it reflects the seriousness of the nature of the disease, as well as gives more significance to the actual disorder so that people don’t feel gaslit about how bad their symptoms are and how much we need to do research on it,” Aslanian said.
While PMOS is chronic and has no cure, treatment options prioritize lifestyle changes and birth control. In an interview with The Daily, Kayla Blaise, a medical resident at Michigan Medicine, said she hopes the reclassification will clarify the rationale behind hormonal treatment options for patients.
“I think it will help people understand that there’s going to be hormonal treatments to this hormonal issue, and one thing that birth control is, is hormonal,” Blaise said. “I always feel bad when patients come in and we’re like, ‘just lose weight and all your problems will get better,’ especially when we know that PMOS actually makes it more difficult to lose weight. … Hopefully this also gives doctors an opportunity to reflect and think on the ways that they can support patients through what is an insulin-resistance and hormonally driven disorder.”
Aslanian said while the name change is significant, it isn’t the final step in increasing awareness and research funding for women’s healthcare.
“Continue investing in women’s health,” Aslanian said. “Invest a lot more than we have in women’s health, not relegate it to the sidelines. Women’s health is not a minority subject. We are half of the population.”
